title: Atomising Fraction Addition
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane shows what atomisation looks like in practice by breaking fraction addition into a sequence of small, secure steps for students who are weak with multiplication facts. He frames the work with three principles: teach one small step at a time, make sure students are fluent with each step before moving on, and explicitly connect the steps. He explains why the least common denominator and multiply-the-denominators methods both load working memory with multiplication, which crowds out thinking about what fractions mean. His sequence moves from adding with common denominators, to asking whether fractions are ready to be added, to generating equivalent fractions by skip-counting, to explaining why they are equivalent with a clock tool, to circling two ready fractions and adding them. Only then does he fade scaffolding. He answers the objection that atomising loses the big picture by arguing that managing cognitive load frees attention for connections, and admits that it demands careful planning and patience.
points: Atomisation rests on three principles: small steps taught one at a time, fluency before moving on, and explicit connections between steps.
Both standard fraction addition methods depend on multiplication, so students with weak facts spend their working memory on arithmetic rather than on what fractions mean.
Kane's atoms run from common denominators and a ready-to-add check, through equivalent fractions, to circling two ready fractions and adding them, before scaffolds are removed.
Reducing the cognitive demand of one atom makes it easier to ask why questions that hold the procedure together and help students remember it.
Practice should be short and spaced over days, with mini whiteboards and Do Nows, rather than twenty problems in a row.
quotes: Take a concept, break it into small pieces, teach one piece at a time, and build up to the larger concept. I find the idea helpful, but I have also found it to be much harder in practice than it sounds.
The core of atomisation, to me, is managing cognitive load. Students have finite working memory capacity: we can only hold a few things in our mind at once.
Students are thinking hard about multiplication, not about the meaning of fractions and why we add them the way we do, which means they’re less likely to retain that learning.
It relies on skip-counting, which my students are pretty confident with, rather than jumping straight to multiplication.
Instead I have them do a few, then the next day check for understanding and do a few more, and continue that until students can reliably remember how to do this the next day.
The second benefit is that, with less cognitive demand, it’s much easier to step back and make connections.
When I don’t break math down into small steps, some students are so overwhelmed that they lose both the details and the big picture.
If I’m managing cognitive load effectively, that frees up mental energy that we can spend making connections and thinking about big ideas.
